::: {.notes}
**Beat 1 · Situation — 35 s**

Shiny has always been a framework for rapid prototyping. You get something
impressive in front of someone fast. A coding assistant accelerates that further.

But no real problem is solved at prototype speed. The work is what comes after:
feature requests, shifting understanding of the problem, fixes layered on
workarounds.

*Consultancy line is credibility, not common ground — one clause, and only if it
buys belief for the demo later.*
:::

::: {.notes}
**Beat 2 · Complication — 35 s**

Play-doh doesn't run out. It just gets browner. Every re-form mixes what used to be
separate, and nothing un-mixes it.

Everything is tailor-made, so nothing carries over to the next project. The logic
you would want to reuse can't be separated from the app it grew inside.

What accelerated is the starting. Every new app still starts from scratch.

*No AI line in this beat — the room joins beat 1 to this image unaided.*
:::

::: {.notes}
**Beat 3 · Question + hook — 20 s**

So: how do you make the next app cheaper than this one?

**By taking things away.** By adding restrictions.

The stud is the trade: the thing that limits what shapes you can build is the same
thing that lets the pieces connect.

You are building an approximation of the perfect shape. When that's acceptable, you
get a material that is far easier to wield.

*Memorable line — one breath, quotable enough to survive to the hallway. Try it
with and without the words on screen.*
:::

## A block {transition="slide-in none-out"}

::: {.placeholder}
[Diagram — block anatomy]{.ph-label}
One or more data inputs, some user parameters, exactly one data output. Contrast
with a Shiny module: arbitrary inputs, arbitrary outputs, side effects, any
communication channel you care to invent.

To generate fresh — the 2025 diagrams predate the current UI. Wants to read as one
picture, not a labelled schematic: the many-armed module beside the block's three
ports.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Beat 4a · The restriction — ~25 s**

A Shiny module can have arbitrary inputs, arbitrary outputs, side effects, and any
communication channel you care to invent.

A block: one or more data inputs, some user parameters, exactly one data output.
That's it. That's the stud.
:::

## A block {transition="none-in slide-out"}

``` r
new_join_block <- function(type = "left", by = character(), ...) {
  new_block(
    server = function(id, x, y) {
      moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
        # ... UI bindings for `type` and `by` ...
        list(
          expr = reactive(
            bquote(
              dplyr::join(x, y, by = .(by), type = .(type))
            )
          )
        )
      })
    },
    ui = function(id) {
      # ... select inputs for join type and join columns ...
    },
    ...
  )
}
```

::: {.notes}
**Beat 4b · The restriction, concretely — ~45 s**

Join block: `x`, `y` in; join type and join columns as parameters; one table out.

*Pseudo-code — replace with the real thing, keep it around a dozen lines, and use
`code-line-numbers` to walk it in three moments (inputs / parameters / the one
output) the way the 2025 deck walked the dplyr pipeline.*

*Biggest time risk in the talk. This is the only place the audience sees what
"build a block" actually means — if it doesn't feel achievable, the ask doesn't
land.*
:::

::: {.placeholder}
[Screenshot — a board]{.ph-label}
Blocks and the links between them, visible as a graph. No text on this slide —
beat 5 carries lines that need to be heard, not read.

Fresh capture of the current UI. The point it has to make visually is *small
vocabulary*: few kinds of thing, connected simply.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Beat 5 · Bridge — 35 s**

Small, well-scoped units of computation with a simple, stable API. So logic lives in
general-purpose blocks; the framework handles communication and reactivity.

The tailoring lives in configuration now, so the code carries over.

A board is a small vocabulary: blocks, and the links between them. That turns
authoring into assembly — and assembly doesn't take a big model.

**This is not an impressive use of AI. That's rather the point.**

*"The code carries over" is the sentence connecting complication to payoff — if it
takes more than one breath, you can't afford both ends of the argument.*

*Don't name the package: blockr.ai is on the way out, blockr.assistant on the way
in. "The assistant" stays true whichever has shipped.*
:::
